reference.source: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
clinicalPearls: The commonest peripheral (non-aortic) arterial aneurysm, defined as focal dilatation of the popliteal artery, commonly more than 50% of the adjacent normal diameter or an absolute diameter typically exceeding around 2 cm.
Strongly associated with male sex, smoking, hypertension and coexisting abdominal aortic aneurysm.
Bilateral in roughly half of cases, and frequently associated with an abdominal aortic aneurysm, so both popliteal fossae and the aorta must be imaged.
Complications are predominantly thromboembolic (acute limb ischaemia, distal embolisation, progressive obliteration of the tibial run-off) rather than rupture, which is uncommon.
A prominent, easily palpable popliteal pulse should raise suspicion; a pulsatile popliteal mass is aneurysmal until proven otherwise.
Presentation ranges from incidental and asymptomatic to intermittent claudication, limb-threatening acute ischaemia, or compressive symptoms such as venous obstruction and neuropathy.
Duplex ultrasound is first-line for diagnosis, sizing and surveillance; CT or MR angiography defines run-off for intervention planning.

Repair, by open bypass with aneurysm exclusion or endovascular stent-grafting, is indicated for symptomatic aneurysms and for asymptomatic aneurysms above a threshold size or with significant mural thrombus or poor run-off.
reference.pathophysiology: The popliteal artery undergoes segmental degeneration of the media with loss of elastin and smooth muscle, collagen remodelling and matrix metalloproteinase-driven wall weakening, mirroring aortic aneurysmal disease. Repetitive flexion at the knee, turbulent flow and mural stress promote progressive dilatation and deposition of laminated thrombus within the sac. The stagnant flow within the redundant lumen favours thrombus accumulation that embolises distally, progressively occluding the tibial run-off, or acutely thromboses the aneurysm to produce severe acute limb ischaemia with a poorly developed collateral bed. Rupture is uncommon because of the confining structures of the popliteal fossa.
additionalDifferentials: Deep vein thrombosis presenting with a swollen, painful calf
Cystic adventitial disease of the popliteal artery
Soft-tissue tumour or sarcoma of the popliteal fossa
Popliteal abscess or enlarged lymph nodes
additionalInvestigations: Duplex ultrasound of both popliteal arteries for diagnosis, size and mural thrombus
Abdominal aortic and iliac ultrasound to exclude coexistent aneurysm
CT angiography of the lower limb
MR angiography as an alternative for run-off assessment
Catheter angiography, frequently with a view to thrombolysis or intervention
Ankle-brachial pressure index and arterial waveform studies
Dedicated imaging of the contralateral limb given the high bilaterality
redFlags: Acute limb ischaemia with the six Ps (pain, pallor, pulselessness, paraesthesia, paralysis, perishing cold), which is limb-threatening.
Sudden loss of previously palpable distal pulses with a cold, painful foot.
Progressive rest pain, tissue loss or trash foot from distal embolisation.
A rapidly enlarging or tender popliteal mass.
Compressive neurological deficit or acute venous outflow obstruction.
reference.prognosis: Asymptomatic aneurysms carry a substantial annual risk of thromboembolic complications, and once acute ischaemia occurs limb loss rates are high, particularly with poor distal run-off. Elective repair before complications develop yields good long-term patency and low amputation rates.
pitfalls: Mistaking a pulsatile popliteal mass for a Baker's cyst and attempting aspiration.
Failing to screen the contralateral popliteal artery and the abdominal aorta.
Underestimating a thrombosed aneurysm because the mass is no longer pulsatile, delaying diagnosis in acute ischaemia.
Delaying repair of an asymptomatic aneurysm harbouring large mural thrombus or compromised run-off.
Attributing calf swelling solely to deep vein thrombosis and anticoagulating without imaging the artery.
references: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
European Society for Vascular Surgery clinical practice guidelines on the management of peripheral arterial aneurysms
management: Elective repair by open bypass with aneurysm exclusion, or endovascular stent-grafting in selected anatomy, for symptomatic, enlarging, or thrombus-laden aneurysms to pre-empt thromboembolic limb loss
Cardiovascular risk reduction with smoking cessation, antiplatelet therapy, a statin and blood-pressure control
Duplex ultrasound surveillance of small asymptomatic aneurysms with preserved run-off
Imaging of the contralateral popliteal artery and the aorta given frequent bilaterality and coexisting abdominal aortic aneurysm
Acute limb ischaemia managed as an emergency with catheter-directed thrombolysis to clear the tibial run-off followed by definitive revascularisation
Referral to vascular surgery for planning of repair and long-term graft surveillance
